verdict.reasoning: Duration and sites: Doctor summarizes 'For the last four days, you've had very itchy skin, very sore skin all over your body, mainly your chest... arms' and patient clarifies 'Just the chest, hands and like, like inside the elbows.' Itch/soreness and impact: Patient: 'it's really itchy... I can't even sleep at night... I can't focus on my work.' Red skin: Patient: 'I have like a sore, and a red skin.'
Patient: 'earlier I was like prescribed for my eczema' and later: 'my eczema was only on the arms.' This supports prior eczema limited to arms.

Previous prescription: 'earlier I was like prescribed for my eczema... they gave me like some cream...' and 'when the symptoms appeared again, I tried those and it didn't work.' OTC steroid: 'I bought a, a steroid cream at the pharmacy last night. But it apparently didn't help, because it's still itching a lot today.'
Patient: 'I have to take like showers every day to be able to, cannot uh ease this itching part, which is very very annoying.' This indicates showers provide some relief.

Dry/cracked: Doctor: 'you mentioned it's, you've got some dry skin and some, uh cracked skin as well.' No pus/blood: Doctor: 'have you noticed any uh bleeding or discharge...' Patient: 'No... my skin is a bit cracked...' Doctor: 'You've not... seen any other uh pus or blood...'; Patient: 'No.'
Denies fever/systemic: Doctor: 'any temperature or fevers?' Patient: 'No. just very itchy. Nothing else.' Doctor further screens bowels, chest, breathing, urine; patient denies problems.
Eczema history: Patient: 'earlier I was like prescribed for my eczema.' Doctor: 'your background of eczema.' This supports a diagnosis of eczema.
Patient: 'I just had asthma in the past. But not anymore.' This supports past, currently inactive asthma.
Doctor: 'do you take any regular medications at the moment?' Patient: 'Uh no.'
OTC steroid use: Patient: 'I bought a, a steroid cream at the pharmacy last night.' This is an over‑the‑counter topical steroid.
Patient: 'Yes, I have tried antihistamines, uh lately, but it didn't really help.' This indicates recent OTC antihistamines with no relief.
Doctor: 'do you have any allergies at all?' Patient: 'Ohh, allergies. Uh, no.'

Age/sex: Doctor repeatedly addresses patient as 'sir' (male); patient: 'you know I'm thirty one.' Living situation: 'I live with a few flatmates.' Job: 'I work uh at a pharmaceutical company... I'm a, like a kind of project manager.'
Smoking: Doctor: 'do you smoke at all?' Patient: 'No.' Alcohol: Patient: 'once in a while... a few, a few beers per week... Nothing, nothing crazy.'

Hiking limited: Patient: 'I like, for instance hiking, during the weekend... I can't really do it anymore, because it's like very like I wanted to do that last weekend. And because super painful...' indicating the rash limits hiking.

Doctor suspects eczema flare: 'I do wonder whether this is a flare-up of your eczema.' Widespread/highly pruritic: 'very itchy skin, very sore skin all over your body, mainly your chest' plus patient reports chest, hands, inside elbows. Refractory to low‑potency OTC steroid: patient used a pharmacy 'steroid cream' that 'didn't help' and prior prescribed creams 'didn't work.'

Doctor: 'I wonder whether giving you a stronger prescription of a of a steroid may be beneficial... which I'm happy to prescribe to you today.' This is a higher‑potency topical corticosteroid compared to OTC.

Doctor: 'I'm going to give you something, some emollients, which helps to moisturize the skin... which use in the bath and shower. And it's definitely worth um using that for the first seven to ten days.'

Doctor: 'I can give you something a little bit stronger today as well. Um, something like Fexofenadine, which I can give to you today. It's definitely worth trying...' This is an oral antihistamine for itch.

Trigger diary and moisturization: Doctor: 'it's also worth keeping a diary of any triggers which are affecting your symptoms, anything you wear or anything you use, in terms of shower gels or soap.' Emollients are specifically to moisturize: 'some emollients, which helps to moisturize the skin.' Regular use implied: 'using the steroids and the emollients, um on a regular basis over the next week to ten days.'
Doctor: 'do come back and see me next week, if things don't get better.' This is follow‑up in about one week if no improvement.
